narration: The Bronx Hop: How Cuba’s Pachanga Conquered New York

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Pachanga originated in Cuba in 1959, with Eduardo Davidson’s song 'La Pachanga' serving as the catalyst for the genre.
It gained massive popularity in New York City post-World War II, particularly within the South Bronx, where Cuban immigrants established a thriving cultural scene.
The Caravana Club is widely regarded as the home of the dance, while the Triton After-Hours Club saw the improvisation of the 'Bronx Hop,' a signature move of the fad.
on_screen: Map: Cuba · Caribbean
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Pachanga was a popular social dance in mid-century Cuban and New York dance halls.
It is described as a 'happy-go-lucky' dance, often associated with festive gatherings and the vibrant nightlife of the era.
In modern contexts, it is primarily performed as part of salsa 'shines'—solo segments within partner dancing.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Pachanga is a grounded dance performed on the downbeat of 4/4 time.
The basic step involves a continuous double-bending and straightening of the knees, which never fully lock.
This movement creates a rhythmic bounce and a gliding effect during weight transfers.
Watch for Bronx Hop.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Solo shines or partner dance.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is played by charanga ensembles, which typically include violins, flutes, and drums.
It is described as a mixture of son montuno and merengue, sharing similarities with the cha-cha-chá but distinguished by a stronger downbeat.
Listen for the violin, flute, drums, piano.
The pulse is 4/4.
A bright, rhythmic sound driven by high-pitched violins and flutes, characterized by repetitive riffs and a persistent, bouncy downbeat.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Eduardo Davidson (composer), José Fajardo (bandleader), Johnny Pacheco (flutist), Eddie Torres (instructor), and the dance group 'Los Pachangueros'.
The dance is still practiced in Cali, Colombia, and has been integrated into global salsa scenes.
Pachanga evolved from Cuban son montuno and merengue and served as a precursor to the development of salsa and boogaloo.
